summary:
Burundi criminalises same-sex conduct. The prohibition dates from the 2009 penal code, and US State Department human rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 record discrimination against gays and lesbians under that framework, together with arrests and harassment of LGBT people. None of the sources cited identifies a decriminalisation measure, exemption or statutory protection for them.

In December 2023 President Évariste Ndayishimiye publicly called for homosexuals to be "stoned", adding "that's what they deserve". Human Rights Watch, reporting on 19 January 2024, described the remarks as stoking fear among LGBT people and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution.

SOS Médias Burundi reported on 4 January 2024 that LGBTQ Burundians said they feared persecution in the wake of the speech. The Iteka League, a Burundian LGBTQ rights organisation operating in exile, characterised the remarks as "a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people". Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the speech as "a real license to kill (us)".
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2015 report places its section on violence and discrimination against LGBT persons inside a documented national crisis that includes extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns. The 2010 and 2012 reports likewise list discrimination against gays and lesbians alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prison conditions and prolonged pretrial detention, so a same-sex conduct arrest would place a visitor inside a custodial system already described in those terms.

The pattern runs across a decade of reporting rather than a single year: the 2009 report covers the year the penal code criminalised same-sex conduct, and the 2010, 2012 and 2015 reports continue to record the same discrimination under the unchanged framework.

The December 2023 presidential remarks are documented by three independently sourced accounts, from Human Rights Watch, SOS Médias Burundi and the Iteka League, each of which reads the speech as an invitation to violence against LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Burundi's best-known LGBTQ rights organisation, the Iteka League, works from exile, and the community members quoted by SOS Médias Burundi spoke to the press only on condition of anonymity, describing a real risk of targeting. Both facts bear on how Burundian LGBT residents can organise, speak publicly or seek redress.

Human Rights Watch directed its appeal to the ruling party, the political actor the sources treat as capable of curbing persecution. No source identifies an independent equality body, ombudsman or dedicated protection mechanism through which a Burundian citizen could report anti-LGBT abuse.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in this material addresses legal gender recognition, changes to sex markers on identity documents, passport or visa screening that could expose a trans traveller's status, access to healthcare, hate-crime provisions, or recognition of same-sex partners or marriages. The findings rest on criminalisation of same-sex conduct and reported anti-LGBT enforcement.

The specific article of the 2009 penal code and its prescribed penalty are not stated in the cited sources, nor is the threshold of proof or the handling of complaints.

Not sourced: whether enforcement differs between Bujumbura and other provinces, and whether the remarks of December 2023 were followed by prosecutions or arrests. The most recent reporting in the inventory is dated January 2024, so later developments are unresolved here.

Not sourced: whether the broader crisis conditions recorded in the 2015 US State Department report persist at present.
